subject: Archaeology
title: Stratigraphy: Reading Earth Like a Book
description: Learn Stratigraphy: Reading Earth Like a Book in one minute.

hook.text: The ground beneath your feet is a stack of layers, each one a page from a different era. Archaeologists read downward.

buildup.text: Stratigraphy is the principle that older layers sit below newer ones.

discovery.text: Each layer is called a context. Changes in soil color, texture, or content signal a new chapter of occupation.

twist.text: Humans constantly disturb layers — pits, ditches, and foundations cut through older deposits, scrambling the book.

climax.text: Harris Matrices diagram the relationships between every context — a flowchart showing what came before what.

punchline.text: The ground is a history book written in dirt.

quiz.question: What is the basic principle of stratigraphy?
options: Lighter soils are always older than darker soils
Older layers sit below newer ones in undisturbed ground
Each soil type corresponds to a specific historical period

details.summary: Stratigraphy is the principle that soil layers accumulate over time, with the oldest at the bottom and newest on top. Archaeologists read these layers like pages in a book, using color, texture, and contents to reconstruct the sequence of human activity at a site.
details.whyItMatters: Stratigraphy is the foundation of archaeological dating and interpretation. Without understanding which layers are older and which are newer, artifacts become isolated objects without historical context or chronological meaning.
takeaways: Older deposits lie beneath newer ones in undisturbed sites
Soil color, texture, and inclusions distinguish different layers
Stratigraphy provides the relative chronology of a site

faq.question: How do archaeologists identify different stratigraphic layers?
faq.answer: Each layer has distinct characteristics — color, texture, compaction, and contents. A destruction layer might be charcoal-rich and black. A floor surface might be compacted and smooth. Changes between layers represent events: building, demolition, flooding, or abandonment.

faq.question: What happens when stratigraphy is disturbed?
faq.answer: Later activities like pit-digging, plowing, or burrowing animals can move objects from one layer to another. Archaeologists look for cut features — edges where one deposit slices through another — to identify and account for these disturbances in their interpretation.
